extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in continuum thermodynamics, continuum mechanics, and PDE theory
extracted.subtask_description: Axiomatic and PDE-based presentation of continuum thermodynamics: kinematics, conservation laws, Clausius–Duhem inequality, constitutive relations (fluids/elastic solids), and entropy-based estimates for elliptic and parabolic PDEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of entropy S and temperature T
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the abstract thermodynamic system satisfies (17). Then there exist continuous functions S : Σ → R and T : Σ → (0, ∞) such that for each process Γ = (ν, µ) ∈ P one has ∫ (dµ)/T ≤ ∫ S dν (inequality (26)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is obtained via Hahn–Banach separation producing φ, ψ ∈ C(Σ) with Φ(ν, µ)=∫ψ dν + ∫φ dµ ≤ 0 on processes and ∫φ dρ > 0 on M1_+(Σ); set S = −ψ, T = 1/φ. Interpret (26) as a form of Clausius' inequality. (See proof for construction and continuity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Clausius inequality for cyclic and reversible processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ∮_Γ d−Q/T := ∫ (dµ)/T for a process Γ = (ν, µ). Then for cyclic processes Γ, ∮_Γ d−Q/T ≤ 0; for a process from α to β, ∮_Γ d−Q/T ≤ S(β) − S(α). Equality holds for reversible processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This repackages (26) into the familiar Clausius inequality (see (29)–(31)). Reversibility is defined by Γ reversible iff its time-reverse ˆΓ ∈ P, yielding equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinematic modeling: motion map χ must be smooth orientation-preserving diffeomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Model motion by χ : U × [0, ∞) → R^3 with x = χ(X,t); for each t, χ(·,t): U → U(t) is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism. The inverse ψ = χ^{-1} gives X = ψ(x,t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption underlies material (Lagrangian) vs spatial (Eulerian) descriptions and justifies definitions of velocity v = ∂_t χ and deformation gradient F = D_X χ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness and sign assumptions for physical fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical fields ρ, e, r, s, θ are taken real-valued and smooth; b, q are R^3-valued; T takes values in S^3. Mass density ρ and temperature θ are assumed positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These regularity and positivity assumptions permit differentiation, integration by parts, and use of constitutive formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Total mass in any material subregion is conserved, yielding the local PDE ∂ρ/∂t + div(ρ v) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is derived by differentiating the mass integral over moving regions (Gauss–Green) and is a basic admissibility requirement for processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of linear momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Rate of change of linear momentum in a moving region equals body force plus contact force: equivalently ρ Dv/Dt = ρ b + div T (balance of momentum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is assumption I and must hold for admissible thermodynamic processes; used together with constitutive relations to determine motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The rate of change of total energy equals mechanical work plus heat supply minus heat flux: ρ De/Dt = ρ r − div q + T : Dv (energy balance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumption II. This identity couples internal energy, stress power, heat supply and flux and is used to constrain constitutive models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clausius–Duhem inequality (continuum form)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any moving region the entropy inequality holds: ρ Ds/Dt ≥ ρ r/θ − div(q/θ), equivalently the local production γ := Ds/Dt − r/θ − (1/ρ) div(q/θ) satisfies γ ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumption III; encapsulates Second Law in local form and is the principal thermodynamic constraint on constitutive relations (positivity of entropy production).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local production of entropy γ nonnegativity and formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Define local production γ per unit mass by γ = Ds/Dt − r/θ − (1/ρ) div(q/θ). Equivalent expanded formulas are given (see (7)). The requirement is γ ≥ 0 for all admissible processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: γ encodes irreversible dissipation; many constitutive restrictions are derived by enforcing γ ≥ 0 for suitably chosen motions and fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible thermodynamic process
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion χ and a collection of fields ρ, T, b, e, q, r, s, θ satisfying I (balance momentum), II (energy balance), and III (Clausius–Duhem inequality) are called an admissible thermodynamic process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutive models and existence results are framed in terms of admissible processes; constructing admissible processes is a tool for deriving constitutive constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive relations for a perfect fluid with heat conduction
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist functions ĕ, ˆθ, ˆT, ˆq such that e = ĕ(s, v), θ = ˆθ(s, v), T = ˆT(s, v), q = ˆq(s, v, Dθ) (where v = 1/ρ is specific volume).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the structural assumptions. To be admissible they must also satisfy implications from Clausius–Duhem, determining temperature, pressure relations and heat conduction inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature and pressure formulas for fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: From Clausius–Duhem one deduces ∂e/∂s = θ (temperature formula) and ∂e/∂v = −p (pressure formula), and the stress T = −p I for a fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations identify thermodynamic conjugate variables and are derived by allowing arbitrary variations in deformation and entropy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat conduction inequality and no heat flow without temperature gradient
rubrics_metrics.description: The heat flux function must satisfy q(s, v, p) · p ≤ 0 for all s, v and p (where p represents Dθ). Moreover ˆq(s, v, 0) = 0 (no flux when Dθ = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from γ ≥ 0 and variation arguments; physically enforces that heat flows from hot to cold (dissipation sign).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive relations for a viscous fluid and dissipation inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist ĕ, ˆθ, ˆT, ˆl, ˆq with e = ĕ(s, v), θ = ˆθ(s, v), T = ˆT(s, v) + ˆl(s, v)[Dv], q = ˆq(s, v, Dθ), leading to T = −p I + l[Dv] and the dissipation requirement l(L) : L ≥ 0 for all L ∈ M_{3×3}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viscous contribution ˆl models internal friction; dissipation inequality enforces nonnegative viscous dissipation. One may scale arguments (λ) to isolate terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material objectivity constraint on viscous tensor (form of l[·])
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle of material objectivity implies l[·] must have the isotropic form l[Dv] = μ(Dv + (Dv)^T) + λ (div v) I, with scalar μ, λ functions of (s, v), and constraints μ ≥ 0, λ + μ ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectivity (frame-indifference) restricts admissible tensorial dependence; the inequalities follow from dissipation inequality and ensure nonnegative dissipation coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navier–Stokes structure as permissible constitutive consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: With constant μ, λ and b ≡ 0, the balance laws produce compressible Navier–Stokes: ρ Dv/Dt = −∇p + μ Δv + (λ + μ) ∇(div v); incompressible limit gives classical incompressible Navier–Stokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows how specific constitutive choices yield canonical PDE models; admissibility requires consistency with Clausius–Duhem and objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive relations for perfect elastic materials and stress formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For elastic solids assume e = ĕ(s, F), θ = ˆθ(s, F), T = ˆT(s, F), q = ˆq(s, F, Dθ); then the stress formula is T = ρ (∂e/∂F) F^T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulas are derived by allowing arbitrary variations in deformation gradient F and entropy; they reduce to fluid formulas in special cases (cofactor relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive relations for viscous elastic materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Viscous-elastic constitutive form: e = ĕ(s, F), θ = ˆθ(s, F), T = ˆT(s, F) + ˆl(s, F)[Dv], q = ˆq(s, F, Dθ), resulting in T = ρ (∂e/∂F) F^T + l[Dv] and dissipation inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines elastic stress with viscous dissipation; same nonnegativity constraints apply to viscous part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipresence principle remark
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutive rules given (e.g., (2),(13),(19),(23)) do not satisfy the general principle of equipresence (a variable present in one constitutive equation should be present in all unless excluded by invariance or physics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modelers should be aware of equipresence as an additional structural principle; see Truesdell–Noll for treatments that enforce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workless dissipation (rigid body) model assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rigid body model set v ≡ 0, b ≡ 0, ρ ≡ 1. Remaining fields e, q, r, s, θ satisfy ∂e/∂t = r − div q and ∂s/∂t ≥ r/θ − div(q/θ), leading to constraints on constitutive dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simplified framework is used to analyze free energy dependence and to deduce that e and s may depend only on θ (not on Dθ) under the given constitutive ansatz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free energy formula and resulting constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Define free energy f = e − θ s. Then ∂f/∂θ = −s (free energy formula) and compatibility with Clausius–Duhem forces D_p ˆf = 0, so e and s do not depend on Dθ; also heat conduction inequality q(θ,p)·p ≤ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations lead to classical thermodynamic identities (analogue of ∂F/∂T = −S) and justify Fourier's law special case q = −A p with A positive semidefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier's law and positivity of conductivity matrix
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourier's law: q(θ,p) = − A p with A symmetric; heat conduction inequality requires p·(A p) ≥ 0 for all p, i.e. A positive semidefinite (a_{ij} ξ_i ξ_j ≥ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard linear constitutive law for heat flux; admissibility requires nonnegative definite conductivity to ensure nonnegative entropy production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptic PDE: entropy identification and internal entropy production
rubrics_metrics.description: For −∑_{i,j} (a_{ij}(x) u_{x_i})_{x_j} = f in U with u>0 and uniformly elliptic A, define internal energy u, entropy log u, and local production γ = ∑_{i,j} a_{ij} u_{x_i} u_{x_j} / u^2 (so γ ≥ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change of variables (v = log u) converts a linear elliptic PDE into a nonlinear form whose quadratic structure in gradients gives improved interior estimates (entropy viewpoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy balance identity for elliptic subregions
rubrics_metrics.description: For any subregion V ⊂ U define F(V)=∫_V f/u dx (entropy supply), G(V)=∫_V γ dx (internal entropy production), R(V)=−∫_{∂V} (1/u) ∂u/∂ν_A dS (entropy flux). Then the entropy balance: F(V)+G(V)=R(V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrating PDE divided by u and applying Gauss–Green yields this balance; useful for bounding entropy production/flux via elliptic estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity estimate: entropy flux bounded by capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: For V ⊂⊂ U the entropy flux satisfies R(V) ≤ Cap_A(V, ∂U) where Cap_A(V, ∂U) = ∫_{U−V} a_{ij} w_{x_i} w_{x_j} dx for w solving the harmonic Dirichlet problem w=1 on ∂V, w=0 on ∂U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows that internal entropy production and flux inside compact subregions are uniformly controlled by geometric/coefficient data, independent of the heat supply magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pointwise interior bound on entropy production when f ≡ 0
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ≡ 0 and V ⊂⊂ U, there exists C (depending on dist(V,∂U) and coefficients) such that γ is bounded pointwise on V by a constant C (i.e. γ(x) ≤ C for x ∈ V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof is technical: set v = log u, manipulate the nonlinear equation for v, derive a differential inequality for γ, and apply cutoff/maximum arguments to obtain interior L^∞ bound on γ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harnack inequality via entropy bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: For each connected V ⊂⊂ U there exists C (depending on U, V, coefficients) such that for any nonnegative solution u of −(a_{ij} u_{x_i})_{x_j}=0 one has sup_V u ≤ C inf_V u (Harnack inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is obtained from the interior gradient/entropy bounds (pointwise bound on γ) and integration of |D log u| control to relate maxima and minima on small balls and cover V by finitely many balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong maximum principle
rubrics_metrics.description: For u ∈ C^2(Ū) solving −(a_{ij} u_{x_i})_{x_j} = 0 on bounded connected U, either min_{∂U} u < u(x) < max_{∂U} u for x ∈ U, or u is constant on U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Harnack inequality and weak maximum principle; standard qualitative property of elliptic equations consistent with entropy-based estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic entropy production identity
rubrics_metrics.description: For parabolic PDE u_t − ∑ (a_{ij} u_{x_i})_{x_j} = f in U_T, with u>0, define S(t,V)=∫_V log u(·,t), F(t,V)=∫_V f/u, G(t,V)=∫_V γ, R(t,V)=−∫_{∂V} (1/u) ∂u/∂ν_A. Then d/dt S(t,V) = F(t,V) + G(t,V) − R(t,V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the time-dependent analogue of elliptic entropy balance; useful to track entropy production/evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy nondecrease under insulated boundary and nonnegative supply
rubrics_metrics.description: If the domain is insulated (∂u/∂ν_A = 0 on ∂U) and f ≥ 0, then S(t) = ∫_U log u(·,t) satisfies dS/dt ≥ 0 (entropy does not decrease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take V = U in the entropy production identity; R(t,U)=0 under insulation. This is a continuum analogue of the Second Law for isolated systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity of ∫ Φ(u) for suitable Φ
rubrics_metrics.description: For smooth Φ : (0, ∞) → R with Φ'(z) ≤ 0 and Φ''(z) ≥ 0, the quantity t ↦ ∫_U Φ(u(·,t)) dx is nondecreasing (and if f ≡ 0 it suffices that Φ'' ≥ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes entropy growth (Φ(z) = − log z). Proof uses convexity and integration by parts showing time derivative ≤ 0 (or ≥ 0 depending on sign conventions).
